issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because the patient is the victim; a plausible trigger would be people resembling the perpetrator(s) or contextual robbery cues. As written, this item conflicts with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling dirty/contaminated is not impossible after robbery, but in this profile it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise center on danger, self-blame, and moral injury rather than sexual violation or disgust-based trauma themes. This makes the appraisal set clinically inconsistent with the trauma context.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'Being naked' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless there was a stripping/sexual humiliation element, which is not suggested elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items point to perpetrator proximity and assault cues, making this vulnerability trigger clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally troubling behaviour during the event, but the rest of the profile reflects victim-focused danger, self-blame, and mistrust rather than any specific morally injurious action. In a mugging/robbery context this item is difficult to justify without corroborating memory/appraisal content about the patient's own behaviour.

vignette: Samantha is a 35-year-old Oceania woman who works as an accountant in a bustling downtown office. She has been married for seven years and had always been known for her outgoing personality until a traumatic event changed everything. One night after work, Samantha was walking home when she was mugged by two men in a dark alley near her apartment building. They demanded her wallet and aggressively shoved her against the wall. The taste of fear lingered as they fled into the darkness, leaving her shaken and alone. Since that night, she has been struggling with severe anxiety and intrusive memories. Samantha’s fears are triggered by specific auditory cues such as footsteps behind or nearby, tactile sensations like unexpected touch, and even seeing someone who resembles the offender. These triggers have led to a cycle of rumination and self-blame. For example, when Samantha hears footsteps following her, she instantly feels overwhelmed by the sensation that it might be the same men from that night. This belief often leads her to dwell on what she could have done differently, like taking a different route home or avoiding dark areas. Samantha has also started deliberately dissociating in response to these triggers, trying to leave her body and blank out whenever an intrusive memory resurfaces. She has come to believe that the world is dangerous and that this event happened because of who she is as a person. Her self-blame intensifies when she thinks about how she might have prevented the attack, leading her into deep rumination. The vividness of the memories, particularly the taste and bodily sensations, exacerbates her distress. When Samantha tastes something similar to what she had during the mugging, it triggers a full-body reenactment of that terrifying night. The memory feels so surreal and unreal that she questions whether it truly happened. This leads her to constantly question her own safety and trust in others. Samantha’s inability to relax even when told she is safe is compounded by her persistent belief that the world is dangerous. She has developed a heightened sense of threat, especially when something takes longer than expected. For instance, if her husband is late coming home from work, she assumes something bad must have happened to him. Her maladaptive strategies like rumination and self-blame further entrench these negative appraisals and threat beliefs. Whenever Samantha revisits the memory or feels threatened by a trigger, she falls into cycles of self-reproach and dissociation, making it nearly impossible for her to trust that any situation is truly safe. These experiences have significantly impacted her daily life. At work, sudden touches from colleagues or unexpected noises set off intense anxiety attacks, leading her to avoid social interactions and collaborative projects. This has strained her relationships both at home and in the office. Samantha’s current state leaves her feeling trapped by these intrusive thoughts and fears. She is finally seeking help because she recognizes that this cycle of fear and self-blame is consuming her life. What frightens her most is the possibility that she will never truly feel safe again, while what she hopes for is a return to a sense of normalcy and peace. Her journey toward healing starts with addressing these deeply ingrained beliefs and triggers, aiming to break free from the cycle of fear and self-blame that has taken over her life.
